description: The lexical grammar: the total correspondence from Unicode source text to either a token sequence or one named source-error condition. This is the single definition of what text is Ajisai source, in the same sense that spec/words.json is the single definition of the vocabulary. It is executable: scripts/lib/reference-lexer.mjs interprets this file and nothing else, and a differential test holds that interpreter to the implementation named below.
totality: Every finite sequence of Unicode scalar values is either accepted as exactly one token sequence or rejected with exactly one condition from sourceErrors. There is no third outcome, and no input is left undescribed.

whitespace.note: Enumerated rather than delegated to a host predicate, because host predicates disagree at the edges. U+FEFF is deliberately NOT whitespace here: it is not in Unicode White_Space, so a byte-order mark is an ordinary name character and a leading BOM glues to the first word. A host regex class that includes U+FEFF (ECMAScript \s does) is wrong for Ajisai.

lineTerminator.note: Only U+000A ends a line for the two rules that care — LineBreak emission and comment extent. U+000D, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 are whitespace and separate tokens, but they do not emit LineBreak and do not terminate a comment. A CRLF file therefore behaves exactly like an LF file, because the CR is absorbed as ordinary whitespace before the LF does the work.

asciiDigit.note: ASCII only. A full-width digit such as U+FF11 is an ordinary name character, so it never enters the numeric grammar.

nameCharacter.definition: Any scalar value that is not whitespace
nameCharacter.note: Ajisai allocates no identifier character class, and no rejected character either. A name is whatever survives to the lexeme rules, which is why Japanese names, '.', '==', '^', '~', ';', '<=', '(', ')' and '|' are all ordinary names with no per-character rule of their own. The only characters a name cannot hold are the four delimiters of `delimiterPairs`, and they are withheld by a whole-lexeme rule rather than a per-character one: a lexeme either is exactly one delimiter or holds none. '(' and ')' were once held in reserve and a bare '|' was a retired form the tokenizer answered by name; nothing selected them but habit from other languages, and both were freed. '{' and '}' were freed with them and then allocated — as delimiters that do something the word rule does not, which is the only ground on which a character is taken.

tokens.carries: the decoded contents between the delimiters

phases.summary: Left-to-right, one word position at a time. positionRules are tried in order at each position; the first whose guard holds consumes.

positionRules.note: Emits LineBreak only when the character is a lineTerminator AND the most recent token is not already a LineBreak, so a run of blank lines collapses to one separator. Consumes exactly one character.

Reached only at a word position, so '#' glued to a preceding lexeme is part of that name and starts nothing. When no real token precedes the comment — the stream is empty, or its last token is a LineBreak — the terminating newline is consumed with the comment, so a whole-line comment does not become a blank line. When a real token precedes it, the newline is left for the whitespace rule and separates statements as usual.
The one sub-grammar that whitespace does not delimit. See stringLiteral below.

Consumes to the next whitespace or end of input. No character is checked for validity on the way, because none is invalid: every scalar value that is not whitespace is a name character, so the completed lexeme is always classified by lexemeRules rather than refused mid-word.

postScan.note: A trailing LineBreak is removed, so a file that ends with a newline denotes the same token sequence as one that does not.

phases.summary: A second pass over the raw text, retained for its precise diagnostics on an unbalanced delimiter of either pair.
phases.note: One stack over both pairs of `delimiterPairs`, which is what lets it name the pair in its message. This pass tracks strings and comments by character rather than by word position, so it sees a quote in the middle of a name as opening a string where the scan phase does not. That makes it a partial check by construction: it is allowed to miss an imbalance, never to invent one, because structuralValidation below runs afterwards on the real tokens and has the final say. A closer that pops the other pair's opener is where it stops rather than reports: the fault is a crossed pair, which is structuralValidation's mismatchedCodeDelimiter, and continuing on a stack that has lost an opener is how a partial pass would start inventing. Its purpose is the better message, not the verdict.

phases.summary: The acceptance gate, over the token sequence rather than the text, shared with the entry point that decodes a stored code value.
phases.note: One stack over both pairs of `delimiterPairs`: a closer whose opener is the other pair's is mismatched, which is how a crossed `[ }` is refused without a condition of its own. Because this runs on tokens, it is reached identically from source and from a Vector being read as code, which is what keeps the two entry points on one structural grammar.

lexemeRules.note: Ordered after the four exact matches, so it catches every remaining lexeme in which a delimiter is glued to anything — '[1', '2]', ']^', '{1', 'a}'. A delimiter is a word like any other and must stand alone; the condition keeps its original name from when '[' and ']' were the only pair.
The whole lexeme must be accepted. This is why no character needs a rule of its own: '1/2' is a number because the entire token parses as one, and '/' is the DIV name for exactly the same reason.
The total fallback. Every lexeme the earlier rules decline is a name, which is what makes the lexeme classification total without an identifier character class.

numericGrammar.anchored: The pattern is anchored at both ends: a lexeme that starts as a number but does not end as one is a name, not a malformed number. '1/2/3' and '5.' are names.
notes: A sign must be followed by an ASCII digit, which is what leaves a bare '-' free to be the SUB spelling and '+' the ADD spelling.

A decimal carries at least one digit on both sides of the point: '0.5' and '5.0' are numbers, '.5' and '5.' are not. The point is therefore never the first or last character of a number, which keeps a lone '.' unambiguously a name.
A rational takes no fraction and no exponent: after the denominator the lexeme must end.

This is the single definition of what text denotes a number. A conversion from Text to a Scalar accepts exactly these lexemes and projects everything else to NIL, so the language has one numeric grammar rather than one per entry point.

stringLiteral.closeRule: A quote closes the literal only when the next character is whitespace or end of input. A quote followed by anything else is content.
notes: Whitespace is the sole token delimiter, so it is the sole string terminator too. This is what lets a string carry an apostrophe ('It''s fine' style content) in a language with no escape character and no second quote spelling.

It is also why a string glued to what follows never closes there: 'foo'[1] and 'foo'bar are unclosed literals, not a string followed by something. The closing quote needs a space after it like every other token boundary.
There is no escape collapsing: a quote kept as content is kept verbatim, so 'foo''bar' is one String whose contents are foo''bar.

sourceErrors.summary: A string literal ran to end of input without a closing quote followed by whitespace.
A lexeme contained a delimiter — '[', ']', '{' or '}' — without being exactly that delimiter.
A VectorEnd token had no matching VectorStart.
sourceErrors.witnessNote: The quote is interior to a name, so the scan phase reads one Symbol and then a VectorEnd. The bracketPrecheck pass tracks quotes by character rather than by word position, so it believes a string opened at the quote and never sees the bracket — which is precisely the partiality the phase documents. Structural validation, running on the real tokens, is what catches it. A witness that bracketPrecheck could also catch would not reach this condition at all.

sourceErrors.summary: A VectorStart token was never closed.
sourceErrors.witnessNote: Same mechanism as mismatchedCodeDelimiter: bracketPrecheck is blinded by the interior quote, so structural validation is the phase that reports.
